Dicke subsystems are entangled
Szilárd Szalay1,2,3 and Péter Nyári1,4
1 Department of Theoretical Solid State Physics, HUN-REN Wigner Research Centre for Physics, Budapest, Hungary
2 Department of Theoretical Physics, University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU, Bilbao, Spain
3 EHU Quantum Center, University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU, Leioa, Biscay, Spain

arXiv:2502.18574v3 [quant-ph] 5 Nov 2025

November 5, 2025

We show that all reduced states of nonproduct symmetric Dicke states of arbitrary number of qudits are genuinely multipartite entangled, and of nonpositive partial transpose with
respect to any subsystem.
Entanglement is the most remarkable manifestation of the nonclassical correlations in quantum systems [1, 2], still puzzling the community for almost
hundred years [3]. Deciding if a mixed quantum state
is entangled or separable is a notoriously difficult
problem, most of the known criteria are necessary but
not sufficient for separability [2, 4, 5]. A particularly
strong separability criterion is the Peres-Horodecki,
or partial transpose criterion [6, 7]. It states that if
a quantum state is separable then its partial transposition is positive semidefinite (PPT), or contrapositively, if the partial transposition of a quantum state
is not positive semidefinite (NPT) then the state is
entangled. Since the reverse implication is not true
in general, there are also entangled states of positive
partial transpose [5, 8–11]. This PPT-entanglement
is considered to be a weaker form of entanglement.
A bipartite quantum state can either be separable or entangled [1, 2, 12], while in the multipartite
case entanglement shows a rich structure with many
exciting features [13, 14]. A natural generalization
of the separable/entangled dichotomy to multipartite
systems is the partial separability classification [15–
20], including the notions of partition-separability, kseparability, k-producibility, k-stretchability [19, 20],
biseparability or genuine multipartite entanglement
(GME). Deciding if a mixed quantum state possesses
a particular multipartite entanglement property is an
even more difficult problem than in the bipartite case.
A particularly interesting problem in the multipartite setting is that the entanglement inside the subsystems does not follow from the entanglement of the
whole system. The paradigmatic example of this
 √is
given by the three-qubit GHZ state |000⟩+|111⟩ / 2
 √
and W state |001⟩+|010⟩+|100⟩ / 3, both of which
are fully entangled, but the two-qubit subsystems of
the GHZ state are separable, while those of the W
state are entangled [21]. Symmetric Dicke states are
Szilárd Szalay: szalay.szilard@wigner.hu
Péter Nyári: nyaripeter@student.elte.hu

the generalizations of the W state, and our result is
the generalization of this.
In this work we consider mixed quantum states arising as reduced states of pure multiqudit symmetric
Dicke states, and we show that these states are genuinely multipartite entangled, moreover, this entanglement is also NPT (not PPT) with respect to any
subsystem. This holds for all nontrivial cases, i.e.,
when there are at least two nonzero occupations in
the Dicke state of the whole system.
Dicke states originally appeared in quantum optics [22], and later, thanks to their simple yet interesting structure, became widely used examples and tools
in the theory of multipartite entanglement. Multipartite entanglement criteria in the vicinity of Dicke
states were formulated [23–26], also based on quantum metrology [27–30], which made possible the experimental detection of multipartite entanglement in
photonic [31] or cold atomic systems [32–35]. Entanglement was also characterized in terms of different entanglement measures in pure Dicke states and
even in the mixtures of symmetric Dicke states in
the qubit [36, 37] and also the qudit [38–42] cases.
Dicke states are also important examples in tomography [43]. Dicke states of small numbers of qubits
were also prepared directly in quantum optical experiments [44–47], different methods of preparation were
worked out also for quantum computers [48–51], and
even the matrix product state form of qudit Dicke
states could be derived explicitly [52].

system S is ξ-separable, that is, separable with respect
to a partition ξ = {X1 , X2 , . . .}, if it is a statistical
mixture of states being product with respect to that

We consider symmetric state vectors1 , contained in
the symmetric subspace of the Hilbert space [53–55].
The classification of multipartite entanglement simplifies significantly for these states, namely, these are
either fully separable or GME [54, 56–58]. This is because every pure decomposition of a symmetric state
consists of symmetric pure states, which are known
to be either fully separable or fully entangled. Consequently, a symmetric state entangled with respect to
any bipartition is GME, and a symmetric state separable with respect to any bipartition is fully separable. In this symmetric multipartite case, the PeresHorodecki criterion (3) takes the form

Otherwise, if there is only one occupation in n, then
the Dicke state and also all the reduced Dicke states
are fully separable pure states |i, i, . . . , i⟩⟨i, i, . . . , i|.
Note that for some small systems, mixtures of Dicke
states are known to be entangled if and only if NPT,
so there is no PPT-entanglement, however, this does
not hold in general [61–63]. PPT-entanglement is considered to be a weaker form of entanglement, based
on that PPT-entangled states are bound-entangled,
that is, no pure entangled states can be distilled from
them [64], and it is conjectured that their Schmidt
number, although scaling linearly with the local dimension [9–11], cannot be maximal. (For qutrits, this
conjecture [65] has been proven [66].) Although we
have seen that the reduced Dicke states are NPTentangled, there are further important open questions
about the strength of this entanglement compared to
the weakness of PPT-entanglement, e.g., regarding
Schmidt number or distillability.
